title: Observable Client-Shaping Contract and Backpressure Playbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

This document defines the Observable Client-Shaping Contract (OCSC) — a small, interoperable set of HTTP headers, telemetry expectations, and runtime behaviors that enable Redwood services and clients to cooperatively shape traffic, signal backpressure, and maintain predictable SLOs under bursty and multimodal workloads. The playbook covers the contract definition, telemetry requirements, runtime enforcement guidance, testing checklist, rollout steps, and ownership.

Goals

- Provide a minimal, explicit client->server contract to communicate priority, cost-sensitivity, and resume checkpoints.
- Ensure runtime observability for shaping decisions so operators can explain, tune, and troubleshoot degradation.
- Standardize backpressure semantics so heterogeneous clients (SDKs, mobile, edge proxies) behave predictably.
- Enable safe progressive rollout with test harnesses and SLO gates.

Scope and non-goals

- In scope: REST/HTTP generation and embedding endpoints exposed by Redwood API (hosted and dedicated).
- Out of scope: internal RPCs between runtime shards (covered by internal gRPC contracts) and private deployment-specific network policies (covered by eng-private-deployments).

Contract surface (HTTP headers and semantics)

1) Client hints (always sent when a client intends to use shaping):
- X-RW-Priority: string (one of "urgent", "interactive", "standard", "background"). Purpose: coarse SLO bucketing for request routing and scheduling.
- X-RW-Cost-Sensitivity: string (one of "high", "medium", "low"). Purpose: informs runtime whether to prefer cheaper model variants or quantized fallbacks under contention.
- X-RW-Resume-Token: opaque base64 string. Purpose: checkpoint token used for streaming/resume semantics; must be treated as best-effort by server.
- X-RW-Client-TTL: integer seconds optional. Purpose: how long client will tolerate retries/rescheduling before returning an error to end-user.

Contract rules (server-side obligations)

- Priority honoring: servers MUST map X-RW-Priority to internal queue classes and expose the mapping on the /introspect endpoint. Default mapping: urgent -> realtime queue (p99 budget), interactive -> low-latency queue, standard -> throughput queue, background -> best-effort. Teams may tune mappings but MUST publish mapping in runtime-architecture documentation.
- Cost-sensitivity: when capacity constrained, the serving runtime SHOULD attempt compatible cheaper model variant if X-RW-Cost-Sensitivity is "high" or "medium" and the result meets eval gates.
- Resume semantics: X-RW-Resume-Token is advisory. If accepted, server returns 202 Accepted with X-RW-Resume-Offer: true and sets Retry-After when queueing. If not supported, server returns X-RW-Resume-Offer: false.
- Failure modes: server MUST return structured error JSON with error_code and hints for remediation. Errors that indicate backpressure should use error_code: "THROTTLED" and include a suggested backoff in seconds.

Telemetry and observability expectations

All services implementing OCSC MUST emit the following telemetry fields with every request (span or metric dimension):
- rw.request.priority: one of [urgent, interactive, standard, background]
- rw.request.cost_sensitivity: one of [high, medium, low, unspecified]
- rw.request.resume_offered: boolean (true if server accepted resume token)
- rw.queue.latency_ms: integer (ms spent waiting before dispatch)
- rw.dispatch.path: one of [fastpath, economized-variant, cached, queued]
- rw.fallback.reason: optional string (e.g. "capacity", "quantization", "model-unavailable")

SLOs and alerting thresholds (recommendations)

- Priority SLOs: p95 end-to-end latency targets by priority class (hosted default): urgent < 100ms, interactive < 250ms, standard < 800ms, background best-effort.
- Queue bloat alert: alert when rw.queue.latency_ms.p99 > 2x priority SLO for any priority class for 5m.
- Fallback surge alert: alert when fallback.rate > 1% of successful requests for 10m and backlog is growing.
- Cost-variant regression: maintain an eval-backed quality threshold; alert if economic fallback variants produce >= 2% drop in top-line metric (ROUGE/accuracy/semantic-similarity) for a monitored prompt set.

Runtime enforcement patterns

- Admission controller: implement a lightweight admission controller that assigns queue class and an admission token. It is the source of truth for rw.dispatch.path. Admission decisions must be idempotent and logged to a sampling trace.
- Soft-fallback policy: prefer returning a compatible economized-variant rather than immediately throttling when X-RW-Cost-Sensitivity allows. The chosen variant must pass a local quality gate (fast e2e evals) before use.
- Global overload mode: when cluster-level CPU/GPU fill > 92% and internal backlog growth > 15%/min, enable overload mode where only urgent and interactive priorities are admitted; standard and background receive THROTTLED with Retry-After.

Client SDK recommendations

- Default hinting: SDKs MUST set X-RW-Priority based on usage pattern (chat UI: interactive, batch job: background).
- Exponential backoff: on THROTTLED responses, clients SHOULD apply exponential backoff guided by Retry-After; respect X-RW-Client-TTL when present.
- Retry idempotency: clients must mark retriable requests with a client-supplied idempotency token header (Idempotency-Key) and avoid replays without checking Resume-Token semantics.

Testing and acceptance criteria

- Unit tests: header parsing and queue assignment logic covered with >= 90% branch coverage.
- Integration tests: synthetic multi-priority load tests that exercise admission controller, fallback path, and resume handshake.
- Quality gate tests: run nightly evals comparing economized variants on representative prompt-sets.
- Chaos test: controlled overload experiments validating global overload mode behavior and observing no p50 regression for urgent priority.

Rolling out OCSC (playbook)

1) Preparation (owner: runtime-team)
- Implement header parsing and telemetry emission in a feature branch behind a feature flag.
- Add a lightweight /introspect API that publishes the priority->queue mapping and current queue lengths.
- Add canary harness that will replay production traces (redwood-trace-replayer).

2) Canary (owner: runtime-team + eng-platform)
- Deploy to 1% of traffic in a single region with feature flag on.
- Run synthetic multi-priority scenarios and validate metrics described under SLOs.
- Verify fallback variants quality gate with sample prompts.

3) Progressive rollout
- 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with minimum 24h observation at each step.
- At each step, verify: queue latency p99 within expected bounds, fallback.rate under 0.5%, error budget consumption for interactive/urgent within planned range.

4) Post-rollout
- Publish operational runbook for oncall with playbook steps for reverting feature flag and throttling inbound traffic from gateways.

Observability runbook (oncall steps)

1) Early signal: queue bloat alert triggers for interactive priority.
- Action: scale admission controller horizontally, verify admission latencies. If not resolvable within 5 minutes, flip soft-fallback throttling to reduce admitted standard/background traffic.

2) Mid signal: fallback surge alert and quality regression.
- Action: pause economized-variant rollout (rollback feature flag), trigger evaluation job to compare gold model outputs vs fallback on precise prompt set, and open incident if regression persists.

3) Severe signal: cluster-level overload mode engages unexpectedly and urgent p50 increases > 2x.
- Action: escalate to SRE lead, activate prewarmed spare capacity circuit (reserve pool), and engage capacity-provisioning runbook.

Ownership and governance

- Primary owner: runtime-team (oncall alias: runtime-oncall).
- Product/PD liaison: API-platform PM.
- Observability steward: eng-platform metrics team.
- Policy reviews: required quarterly or after any incident involving backpressure behavior.

Appendices

A. Example request and server response

Request (client):
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Content-Type: application/json
X-RW-Priority: interactive
X-RW-Cost-Sensitivity: medium
X-RW-Client-TTL: 30
X-RW-Resume-Token: YmFzZTY0LXJ1bm5lcg==
{ "input": "Summarize the release notes for the last quarter" }

Server (accepted & queued):
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json
X-RW-Resume-Offer: true
Retry-After: 3
{ "status": "queued", "queue_position": 12, "estimated_wait_s": 3 }

Server (fastpath):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
{ "output": "...summary...", "variant": "economized-v2" }

B. Example metric ingestion labels (Prometheus exemplar semantics)
- rw_request_priority{priority="interactive"}
- rw_dispatch_path{path="economized-variant"}
- rw_queue_latency_ms{priority="interactive",quantile="0.99"}

C. Quick checklist before merging to main
- Feature flag guarded and documented.
- Integration tests using redwood-trace-replayer pass.
- Telemetry emitted and dashboards created in grafana under runtime/ocsc.
- SLOs for each priority class defined in the SLO registry.

Related work and references

- See /architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/telemetry-ingestion-and-retention-guidelines-2025 for metric retention expectations.
- See /architecture-and-standards/api-standards/request-priority-and-hinting-protocol-playbook-2026 for historical rationale on priority classes.
